## Program Design & Activities (~800 words)

**Theory of change.** Our program rests on a straightforward logic: when adults who read below a functional level receive consistent, contextualized literacy instruction paired with workforce-readiness supports and employer engagement, they gain the foundational skills needed to secure and retain entry-level employment, support their children's education, and participate more fully in civic life. Inputs—trained volunteer tutors, evidence-based curricula, employer partnerships, and wraparound referrals—produce activities (structured tutoring, workforce-literacy workshops, and supervised job-readiness practice) that generate short-term outcomes (measurable reading-level gains, document-use proficiency, and completed job applications) and longer-term outcomes (employment, wage increases, and sustained family literacy behaviors). A one-page logic model is included as Attachment [X].

**Core activities.** The program delivers three interconnected activities, each linked to the need and gap documented above.

*Activity 1 — Contextualized one-on-one and small-group tutoring.* Volunteer tutors, trained in [evidence-based methodology, e.g., ProLiteracy's New Readers approach or the STAR reading framework], will deliver 90-minute tutoring sessions twice per week over 24-week cycles, for a total dosage of approximately 72 contact hours per participant per cycle. Sessions will use workplace-contextualized materials—safety manuals, employee handbooks, benefits forms, and job applications sourced from local employer partners—so that skill gains transfer directly to employment settings. Research supports this approach: a [Year] meta-analysis by [Author/Organization] found that contextualized adult literacy instruction produces reading gains [X]% greater than generic curricula and significantly improves learner persistence ([Citation]). Each tutor will work with no more than three learners at a time to maintain individualized pacing. Sessions will be offered mornings, evenings, and Saturdays at [number] neighborhood sites chosen for transit access, directly addressing the scheduling and transportation barrier cited by 64% of survey respondents.

*Activity 2 — Workforce-literacy workshops.* Once per month, participants will attend a three-hour workshop focused on a specific job-readiness skill grounded in literacy: completing employment applications, interpreting pay stubs and benefits documents, reading workplace safety signage, writing email correspondence, or navigating online job portals. Workshops will be co-designed with employer partners—including Harborview Manufacturing Co. and [Partner 2]—to ensure content reflects actual hiring processes and workplace expectations. Each workshop will culminate in a practice task scored against a simple rubric, giving participants and staff a tangible benchmark of progress. Over a 24-week cycle, each participant will complete six workshops (18 contact hours). Employer-contextualized workforce programming aligns with recommendations from the National Coalition for Literacy ([Year]) and mirrors models that have demonstrated [outcome] in [comparable city/program] ([Citation]).

*Activity 3 — Supervised job-readiness practice and employer connection.* In the final four weeks of each cycle, participants who have met minimum reading-level benchmarks will enter a structured job-readiness phase. Staff will facilitate mock interviews with volunteer employer representatives, guide participants through live online job applications, and coordinate informational visits or job shadows at partner worksites. [Organization] will maintain a referral agreement with [Workforce Development Board / American Job Center / Partner] to connect completers with job placement services, interview coaching, and credentialing programs. This phase converts literacy gains into employment action and gives employer partners early access to a pipeline of candidates they have helped prepare—a reciprocal value proposition that sustains employer engagement beyond the grant period.

**Evidence base.** The program model draws on three bodies of evidence. First, structured volunteer tutoring using validated curricula has been shown to produce average reading gains of [X] grade levels over [hours] of instruction ([Citation]). Second, contextualized and workforce-integrated literacy programming improves both skill acquisition and employment outcomes compared with traditional classroom instruction ([Author, Year]; [Author, Year]). Third, programs that embed employer engagement from design through placement report higher learner motivation, lower attrition, and stronger post-program employment rates ([Citation]). Our prior cohort data support these findings: in [Year], [X]% of participants who completed our tutoring cycle achieved at least a [benchmark] reading-level gain, and [X]% secured employment within [time] of exit.

**Participant pathway.** Every learner follows a clear four-stage path.

*Intake and assessment (Weeks 1–2).* Prospective participants are referred by partner organizations, employer HR departments, or self-referral. Staff conduct a standardized reading assessment ([tool, e.g., TABE or CASAS]), a brief needs screening covering transportation, childcare, and work schedule, and a goal-setting conversation. Learners are matched to a tutor and session schedule.

*Core instruction (Weeks 3–20).* Participants attend twice-weekly tutoring sessions and monthly workforce-literacy workshops as described above. Staff conduct a mid-cycle reassessment at Week 12 to adjust pacing and materials.

*Job-readiness bridge (Weeks 21–24).* Participants meeting benchmarks enter supervised job-readiness practice and employer-connection activities. Those needing additional instruction are offered a second cycle with an updated learning plan.

*Follow-up (Months 7–12).* Program staff contact every completer at 30, 60, and 90 days post-exit to track employment status, wage changes, and continued learning. Data are recorded in [database/system] and reported quarterly. Participants who have not yet secured employment are re-referred to workforce partners.

This pathway ensures that no learner exits without a next step—whether that is employment, continued education, or a warm referral—and that outcome data are captured consistently for evaluation and reporting.

## Evaluation Plan (~400 words)

**Design.** The program uses a single-group pre/post design as its primary evaluation framework. We will use pre/post TABE scores and employer-verified employment checks at 30/60/90 days to assess impact. Every participant is assessed at intake, mid-cycle, and exit using the same instrument and scoring protocol, producing three measurement points per learner from which individual and cohort-level gains are calculated. Where feasible, we will pursue a quasi-experimental comparison by requesting de-identified aggregate outcome data from [City/County adult education consortium or partner provider] for learners of similar demographics and baseline reading levels served during the same period. This comparison would allow us to contextualize our gain and employment rates against a non-equivalent control group. We acknowledge the limitations of this approach—selection bias and differing dosage—and will report any comparison findings with appropriate caveats. If a comparison dataset cannot be secured, we will benchmark results against National Reporting System state averages and published outcome data from comparable workforce-literacy programs ([Citation]).

**Data sources and tools.** Each outcome objective maps to a specific instrument. Literacy gain (Objective 1) is measured by the TABE or CASAS reading assessment, administered at Weeks 1, 12, and 24. Workforce document proficiency (Objective 2) is measured by the employer-co-developed workshop rubric, scored at each of six workshops. Employment placement (Objective 3) is measured by participant self-report at 30-, 60-, and 90-day follow-up, verified by pay stub or written employer confirmation. Learner persistence (Objective 4) is measured by session-level attendance logs recorded in [database]. Output indicators—enrollment counts, contact hours, workshops delivered, tutors trained—are captured through intake forms, sign-in sheets, and training rosters.

**Analysis approach.** Literacy gain rates will be calculated as the percentage of completers achieving at least one educational functioning level increase on TABE/CASAS, using matched pre/post scores. Employment placement rates will be calculated as the percentage of participants unemployed at intake who report verified employment within 90 days of exit. We will use an intent-to-treat frame for transparency, reporting outcomes for all enrollees and separately for the completer subgroup (those meeting the 80% attendance threshold defined in Objective 4). For attrition and missing data, participants who exit before Week 24 without a post-test will be counted as non-gainers in the intent-to-treat calculation; the Site Coordinator will attempt to administer an abbreviated exit assessment for any learner who withdraws after Week 12. Follow-up non-response will be addressed through up to three contact attempts by phone, text, and email before a case is coded as "unable to verify."

**Sample size considerations.** With a Year 1 enrollment target of [number] adults across two cohorts, we anticipate [number] completers based on our 65% persistence target. This completer sample is sufficient to detect meaningful descriptive patterns in gain rates and employment placement and to report outcomes with confidence to the funder, though it is not large enough to support complex inferential statistics. We will note this limitation in all reports and use effect-size estimates rather than statistical significance as the primary indicator of program impact. If the program scales in subsequent years, we will revisit the feasibility of a more rigorous evaluation design with a larger sample.

**Data quality, privacy, and storage.** The Site Coordinator enters participant data into [database/system] within 48 hours of each assessment or follow-up contact. The Data and Evaluation Assistant conducts monthly audits, checking a random 20% of records against source documents (paper assessments, sign-in sheets, verification letters) and flagging discrepancies for correction. All participant data are stored in a password-protected, encrypted system accessible only to authorized program staff. Participants provide written informed consent at intake, covering data collection, use for evaluation and funder reporting, and the option to withdraw consent at any time without affecting services. No personally identifiable information is included in external reports; all data are reported in aggregate or with de-identified case examples.

**Roles and reporting cadence.** The Data and Evaluation Assistant prepares quarterly data summaries. The Program Director reviews them with the full team and submits required reports to the funder on [funder's schedule, e.g., quarterly and annually]. If the budget permits, [Organization] will contract with [external evaluator or university partner] to conduct an independent year-end review of data quality and outcome findings, adding a layer of credibility for the funder and for future proposals. That determination will be finalized during Month 1 budget reconciliation.

**Continuous improvement loop.** Evaluation is not an end-of-year exercise. The monthly all-staff data review described in Section 5 serves as the primary learning loop: if attendance trends, mid-cycle assessment results, or follow-up employment rates fall below quarterly benchmarks, the team identifies root causes and implements adjustments—schedule changes, additional tutor support, revised workshop content—within 30 days. Mid-cycle reassessment at Week 12 functions as a built-in course correction for individual learners and for the program as a whole. Findings from each cohort cycle directly inform tutor training content, employer workshop design, and outreach strategy for the next cohort, creating a structured rhythm of reflection and adaptation across the full grant period.
